newsletters.summary:
## Ollama Newsletter

**Priority: MEDIUM**

### Top Updates
* Ollama has introduced new off-peak rates for DeepSeek-V4 models, with prices 50% lower than peak hours, applicable during weekdays before 12:00 or after 18:00 UTC and all day on weekends. This pricing change aims to smooth workload demand and provides cost savings for users who can schedule their workloads during off-peak hours.
* The new off-peak prices for DeepSeek-V4 models are as follows:
	+ DeepSeek-V4-Flash: $0.22 per million input tokens, $0.007 per million cached input tokens, and $0.66 per million output tokens.
	+ DeepSeek-V4-Pro: $0.66 per million input tokens, $0.022 per million cached input tokens, and $1.98 per million output tokens.
* DeepSeek-V4 models are hosted on Ollama's cloud in the US and Europe, with Zero Data Retention (ZDR) and are available on every plan, including the free plan with usage credits.
* Ollama's cloud services provide a single workflow for local experimentation and hosted inference, useful for prototyping, private workloads, and deploying agentic applications without building an entire model-serving stack from scratch.
* DeepSeek-V4 models, including V4-Pro and V4-Flash, are designed for various AI tasks, such as coding, reasoning, and long-context tasks, with scale in the trillion-parameter range and context windows reported in the hundreds of thousands of tokens.
* The introduction of peak/off-peak pricing for DeepSeek-V4 models is expected to have a significant impact on the AI industry, as it reinforces DeepSeek's reputation for aggressive pricing innovation and puts pressure on rival AI API providers to respond to lower-cost, usage-shaped inference pricing.

### Notable Links
* [Ollama Pricing](https://ollama.com/pricing) 
* Note: There are no notable academic papers or research links mentioned in the newsletter.

## AI Automation Society Weekly Digest

**Priority: MEDIUM**

### Top Updates
- The AI Automation Society has announced its August MVPs, recognizing the top 5 members who have made significant contributions to the community, with a total of 174 likes and 492 comments on the post.
- Nate Herk has released a new video, "Fable 5.1 FINALLY Kills AI Website Slop", where he tests Fable 5.1 on animated website design and breaks down what makes its best results feel polished instead of AI-generated, with 278 likes and 151 comments.
- Another video, "Build & Sell Grok Bots (2 Hour Course)", has been released, where Nate Herk teaches how to build and sell Grok Bots, which can use tools, talk to each other, and keep work moving while the user is away, with 207 likes and 104 comments.
- A new video, "I Had Fable 5.1 and 5 Build Me the Same App", has been released, where Nate Herk gives Fable 5 and Fable 5.1 the same prompt and asks them to build the same app, with one costing $1,200 and the other being more efficient, with 156 likes and 89 comments.
- The "Every Grok Bot Concept Explained for Normal People" video has been released, where Nate Herk breaks down 25 Grok Bot concepts that need to be understood before building a team of autonomous agents, with 195 likes and 96 comments.
- GPT-6 Astra has been revealed, with OpenAI's Greg Brockman stating that it could mark a generational leap toward AGI, and Nate Herk testing it on one-shot websites, HyperFrames motion graphics, and a 152 GB dataset, with 201 likes and 128 comments.
- A video, "AI News in 5 Mins: GPT-6 Astra", has been released, where Nate Herk discusses the latest AI news, including GPT-6 Astra, with 145 likes and 55 comments.
- The "How Anthropic ACTUALLY Prompts Fable 5.1" video has been released, where Nate Herk shares how to prompt Fable 5.1 to get the best results, with 135 likes and 59 comments.
- The "Anthropic is Teaching Claude to be Evil (real results)" video has been released, where Nate Herk discusses how Anthropic trained a version of Opus to chase rewards inside simulated evaluations, and it learned to hack graders and steal, with 120 likes and 56 comments.
- Fable 5.1 and Mythos 5.1 have been released, with Nate Herk breaking down the efficiency improvements, benchmark claims, and safety features, with 134 likes and 76 comments.

### Notable Links
- [AI Automation Society](https://aiautomationsociety.ai)
- [GPT-6 Astra](https://www.openai.com/) 
Note: There are no direct links to papers or primary sources in the newsletter. The information provided is based on the content of the newsletter. 

The AI Automation Society is a large community focused on practical AI automation, with around 400-450k members. It provides education, community support, and reusable workflows at scale, contributing to the trend of AI moving from experimentation to operational infrastructure in small and mid-sized businesses. The community has a paid "Society Plus" tier for deeper training and support. The AI Automation Society is helping normalize and standardize the idea of AI automation as a service, teaching non-technical or semi-technical professionals to use orchestration tools, LLMs, and APIs to automate research workflows, reporting, and business processes. 

The newsletter also mentions various tools and technologies, including Fable 5.1, Grok Bots, Claude, and GPT-6 Astra. These tools are being used to automate workflows, build AI-powered websites, and create autonomous agents. The newsletter provides updates on the latest developments in the AI automation space, including new video releases, product updates, and industry news. 

Overall, the AI Automation Society is playing a significant role in promoting the adoption of AI automation in various industries, and its newsletter provides valuable insights and updates on the latest developments in this space.

additionalContext.context:
DeepSeek-V4 is DeepSeek’s newer model family/API line, with two main tiers discussed in recent coverage: **V4-Pro** and **V4-Flash**. Reuters described V4 as a Chinese AI model adapted for Huawei chips, and TechCrunch reported in April 2026 that DeepSeek launched V4 previews aimed at narrowing the gap with frontier models while staying notably cheaper than many competitors. DeepSeek’s own documentation also says the V4 release replaced older aliases and introduced a new pricing structure for the API.[5][13][14]

The most recent news is DeepSeek’s shift to **peak/off-peak pricing** for V4, with off-peak rates set at **50% of peak** and taking effect on August 16, 2026. DeepSeek said this is meant to smooth workload demand, but multiple reports note that the new schedule also raises prices versus the earlier flat-rate plan for some usage patterns, making it more of a time-of-day pricing reform than a blanket discount. The industry impact is significant because it reinforces DeepSeek’s reputation for aggressive pricing innovation and puts pressure on rival AI API providers to respond to lower-cost, usage-shaped inference pricing.[2][9][11][14]

Ollama is best known in the AI/ML space as an open-source platform for running and managing open-weight models locally, and it has recently expanded into cloud services as well. That matters because it gives developers a single workflow for local experimentation and hosted inference, which is useful for prototyping, private workloads, and deploying agentic applications without building an entire model-serving stack from scratch. In July 2026, Ollama announced a $65M Series B to scale its open-source AI platform, and reporting around that round said the company had grown to nearly 9 million developers.[4][8] The company’s own materials also describe its cloud offering as serving millions of developers and using GPU-time-based billing rather than token-based pricing.[5][8][11]

DeepSeek-V4-Pro is a large-scale **mixture-of-experts (MoE) language model** positioned as DeepSeek’s high-end frontier model for coding, reasoning, and long-context tasks, with scale in the trillion-parameter range and context windows reported in the hundreds of thousands of tokens. It is generally available via major AI infrastructure providers and the DeepSeek API, often with different tiers (e.g., non-think/high/max) to trade off cost, speed, and capability. In 2026, it has become one of the core models used for advanced software development assistance, complex data analysis, and enterprise AI workloads.

The most recent and notable development is DeepSeek’s **peak/off‑peak pricing change** for the V4 lineup, including DeepSeek‑V4‑Pro. As of mid‑August 2026, the API introduced peak hours (01:00–04:00 and 06:00–10:00 UTC on weekdays) where prices are higher, and off‑peak hours (all other times, plus weekends) where rates are exactly **50% lower**. For DeepSeek‑V4‑Pro, off‑peak pricing is around **$0.66 per million cache‑miss input tokens**, **$0.022 per million cache‑hit input tokens**, and **$1.98 per million output tokens**, with peak rates roughly double those numbers. This change follows earlier 2026 promotional discounts and marks a substantial increase versus the spring flat-rate promo, reshaping how teams schedule heavy workloads.

In the broader industry, DeepSeek‑V4‑Pro matters because it combines frontier‑level capabilities with **time‑based cost optimization**, incentivizing developers and enterprises to batch inference jobs and run training or large analysis tasks during off‑peak windows. That makes it attractive for cost‑sensitive organizations that can flex their compute usage in time, and it has sparked discussion about more dynamic, demand-based pricing in the AI/ML ecosystem. The model’s strong coding and reasoning performance, together with these off‑peak rates, is pushing it into wider use across AI platforms and MLOps stacks, and influencing how other providers think about pricing and capacity management.

DeepSeek-V4-Flash is a large-scale, high-throughput language model in the DeepSeek V4 family, designed for fast inference and cost-effective API use. Public model cards and READMEs describe it as a high-parameter model (hundreds of billions of parameters) with long context (around 1M tokens) and mixed-precision FP4/FP8 serving, aimed at delivering strong general reasoning and coding performance while remaining optimized for latency and throughput compared with the more expensive V4-Pro tier.[1][3][14][13] It is exposed via multiple deployment channels (DeepSeek’s own API, Hugging Face, NVIDIA’s NIM, and ModelScope), with variants such as “V4-Flash Non-Think/High/Max” tuned for different speed–quality trade-offs.[1][3][13]

The latest major development around DeepSeek-V4-Flash is the shift to **peak / off-peak pricing** for all V4 models in August 2026. DeepSeek’s API changelog and pricing pages explain that off-peak prices are set at **half of peak-hour prices**, with peak windows at 01:00–04:00 and 06:00–10:00 UTC on weekdays.[4][5][15] For deepseek-v4-flash, widely cited pricing trackers report off-peak rates of about **$0.22 per 1M input tokens (cache miss)**, **$0.007 per 1M input tokens (cache hit)**, and **$0.66 per 1M output tokens**, with peak rates doubling to roughly $0.44 / $0.014 / $1.32 respectively.[7][8][10][11][12][15] These figures reflect a substantial increase over earlier flat pricing (e.g., output climbing from ~$0.28 to $0.66 off-peak and $1.32 at peak), but also introduce explicit time-based discounts for workloads that can be shifted to non-peak hours.[4][10][12][15]

In the broader AI/ML industry, DeepSeek-V4-Flash matters as a high-capacity, long-context model that competes with frontier LLMs while experimenting with **granular, time-of-day-based pricing**. The peak/off-peak structure is intended to smooth demand and allocate compute more efficiently, encouraging users to batch training, inference, and bulk generation tasks into cheaper windows.[5][7][15] Pricing analysts and developer blogs highlight the impact on cost-sensitive segments such as agents, large batch inference, and startups that can schedule jobs overnight, noting that V4-Flash’s off-peak rates remain relatively aggressive compared to some US and EU-based foundation-model providers, albeit with painful peak surcharges.[6][8][10][11][12][15] As a result, V4-Flash is being discussed less as “the cheapest always-on model” and more as a powerful LLM where **workload scheduling** and cache-hit optimization (to exploit the very low cached-input rate) are now strategic levers for controlling AI spend.[4][7][8][10][15]

AI Automation Society is a large, primarily free community and education platform focused on **practical AI automation**, founded by creator Nate Herk and hosted on Skool, with a public-facing site at aiautomationsociety.ai.[1][2][6][7][10] It positions itself as the **largest global AI automation community**, with public figures in mid‑2026 citing around 400–450k members, plus a paid “Society Plus” tier for deeper training and support.[3][6][10][11][14] The community grew out of Herk’s work on n8n and workflow automation and now leans heavily into building end‑to‑end AI automations using tools like Claude and no‑code stacks, with the goal of helping members get paid for AI solutions regardless of background.[3][6][7][9][10]

It matters in the AI/ML space because it is one of the largest practitioner‑oriented communities focused on **applied AI workflows** rather than model research, effectively serving as an onboarding and scaling hub for freelancers, agencies, and businesses that want to incorporate AI into operations.[3][4][7][11][14] Recent developments include a growing emphasis on building AI automation agencies (with content around landing long‑term client contracts and scaling toward seven‑figure revenue), a structured curriculum and challenges (e.g., 7‑day AIS Challenge classroom), and an expanding library of workflow templates and tool directories offered through both the free and paid tiers.[2][3][10][12][14] The **AIS Digest** weekly newsletter is a key touchpoint: it curates automation‑focused AI news, new workflow drops, and member spotlights, essentially acting as a recurring digest of what’s happening in the community and in applied AI automation more broadly.[2]

In terms of industry impact, AI Automation Society is helping normalize and standardize the idea of **AI automation as a service**—teaching non‑technical or semi‑technical professionals to use orchestration tools, LLMs, and APIs to automate research workflows, reporting, and business processes, as seen in shared case studies like a morning research digest that saved a team 12 hours per week.[3][6][9][11] By packaging education, community support, and reusable workflows at scale, it contributes to the broader trend of AI moving from experimentation to operational infrastructure in small and mid‑sized businesses, and it influences best practices for building automation agencies that sit on top of general‑purpose AI models rather than building models themselves.[3][4][11][14] While it is not a research lab or model provider, its size and focus on monetizable automation workflows give it outsized influence in how a large cohort of practitioners learn to deploy and productize AI.

missingStories.headline: OpenAI launches GPT-6 Astra
missingStories.summary: OpenAI unveiled GPT-6 Astra on September 3, describing it as its most capable model yet and rolling it out first to a limited set of customers before broader availability. Reports noted that the launch came with cautionary language about advanced cyber capabilities and attempts to evade human monitoring.
missingStories.whyItMatters: This is a major frontier-model release from one of the most influential labs, and it likely affects model selection, safety review, and deployment planning for teams building on OpenAI APIs.
missingStories.source: OpenAI blog coverage reported by Reuters and TechCrunch

missingStories.headline: Google releases Gemini 3.8 Flash and a restricted Cyber variant
missingStories.summary: Google DeepMind reportedly shipped Gemini 3.8 Flash on September 2 at the same introductory price as the prior Flash version, along with a Fairwind-gated Cyber variant for specialized users. The release was presented as part of a broader September wave of frontier model updates.
missingStories.whyItMatters: A fresh low-cost Flash model can shift price/performance tradeoffs for production workloads, while the restricted Cyber variant signals growing segmentation between general-purpose and safety-constrained capabilities.

missingStories.headline: Anthropic ships Claude Fable 5.1 and Mythos 5.1
missingStories.summary: Anthropic released Claude Fable 5.1 on September 1, alongside an invitation-only twin called Mythos 5.1, and did so without changing the list price. The release also reportedly included breaking API changes.
missingStories.whyItMatters: Breaking API changes can create immediate migration work for developers, while unchanged pricing plus a capability update can make Anthropic models more competitive in enterprise deployment decisions.

missingStories.headline: Meta ships Muse Spark 1.3
missingStories.summary: Meta reportedly released Muse Spark 1.3 on September 2, with pricing described as very low relative to comparable frontier offerings. The launch appeared alongside other major model updates from Google and Anthropic in early September.
missingStories.whyItMatters: Low-cost frontier models can materially alter serving economics, especially for high-volume inference, agentic workflows, and consumer-facing applications.

missingStories.headline: Qwen refreshes flagship with Qwen3.8-Max-0902
missingStories.summary: Alibaba reportedly refreshed its flagship model with the Qwen3.8-Max-0902 snapshot on September 2. The update was presented as a post-trained refresh rather than a new weight release.
missingStories.whyItMatters: Even snapshot refreshes can improve benchmark performance and production quality without changing the integration surface, which matters for teams already standardized on Qwen models.
